title: Dasharatha's sacrifice
hook: a demon king who asked for protection from everyone except people
carry: four sons, born to answer a boast

segments.voice: Yesterday: Dasharatha's sacrifice, and your line, where he goes, rain follows. Rishyashringa came, and a horse was set free for a year.

While the priests on earth pour offerings into Dasharatha's fire, the gods hold a meeting of their own. They go to Brahma with a complaint. Ravana, king of the rakshasas, is tormenting all the worlds, and nobody can stop him. Why not? Because Brahma himself gave him a boon. Ravana asked never to be killed by gods, or demons, or celestial beings of any kind. He listed nearly everyone, and left out one group, because he thought them too weak to bother with.
screen: `THE GODS HOLD A MEETING.` → `RAVANA'S BOON.` → `HE LEFT OUT ONE GROUP.`

segments.voice: Ravana left out human beings. He scorned them. So Brahma says: he can be killed by a human. And Vishnu arrives, and agrees to be born as a man, in four parts, as the four sons of Dasharatha. Down on earth, Rishyashringa begins a second rite, for the sake of sons. Out of the fire rises a great shining being, carrying a golden vessel with a silver lid. Inside is payasa, sweet rice cooked in milk, made by the gods. Give this to your queens, he tells Dasharatha. The king, overjoyed, divides it. Half to Kausalya. Of the rest, a share to Sumitra, then a share to Kaikeyi, then the last share to Sumitra again. In time, four sons are born. Rama to Kausalya, on the ninth day of the bright half of the month of Chaitra, the day Hindus still celebrate as Rama Navami. Bharata to Kaikeyi. And to Sumitra, with her two shares, twins: Lakshmana and Shatrughna. The loophole is the whole point: a king who torments every world will be undone by the one thing he thought didn't count. Now the week, from the top. Narada's whole story in one chapter. The poet from the anthill. A krauncha bird, and grief becoming verse. Brahma's promise and the singing twins. A king who asked for help. A rain-bringing sage. And today, four boys, born to answer a boast.
screen: `RAVANA SCORNED HUMAN BEINGS.` · `A VESSEL OF PAYASA FROM THE FIRE.` · `FOUR SONS, AND RAMA NAVAMI.` · `THE WEEK, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `RAMA, BHARATA, LAKSHMANA, SHATRUGHNA.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something small you've been treating as if it doesn't count: a quiet habit, an ordinary friend, a few minutes of breathing a day. Hold it gently, and breathe as if it matters. If you pray, you can give thanks for one ordinary thing.
Dasharatha's sacrifice. Its fruit is the payasa from the fire, shared among three queens, and four sons, born to undo Ravana's boast.
Your line: four sons, born to answer a boast. Ravana never counted on humans. A week, done.

howItsDone: Hindus celebrate Rama Navami, Rama's birthday, on the ninth day of the bright half of Chaitra, with fasting, temple worship, readings of the Ramayana, and in some places a cradle for the infant Rama.

original.note: Sanskrit pāyasa: rice cooked in milk, a sweet pudding. still made for festivals as payasam or kheer.

what a scholar hears: Bala Kanda 15–18 interleave the gods' council with the rite for sons; the payasa division gives Sumitra two shares, and Rama's birth is placed under the Punarvasu star in Chaitra.

chat.says: If Ravana was so powerful, how could a human ever defeat him?
options: His boon left out humans, because he scorned them. So Vishnu was born as a man.
Brahma took back Ravana's boon after the gods complained about him.

chat.meaning: Ravana asked never to be killed by gods or demons, and left out humans. So Vishnu agrees to be born as Dasharatha's four sons.

notes: Week end: the teach looks back over days 491–497.
The order and size of the payasa shares are paraphrased (half to Kausalya; Sumitra two shares; Kaikeyi one); recensions differ in the exact fractions. Confirm.
Rama's birth: ninth day (navami) of the bright half of Chaitra, under Punarvasu; confirm.
Bharata is born after Rama and the twins after Bharata in most tellings; the script lists them in that order without stating it as a sequence.
